◫Lesson 3

Permissible Financial Interests and Your Disclosure Responsibilities

In this lesson, you'll focus on financial interests, including what may be accepted, what must be disclosed, and how these requirements help promote fair, ethical, and compliant business practices.

In Lesson 2, you explored conflicts of interest and learned why identifying, disclosing, and managing them is important.

Now, you'll continue your journey through the regulatory requirements and standards that apply to Representatives and Key Individuals.

In this lesson, you'll focus on financial interests, including what may be accepted, what must be disclosed, and how these requirements help promote fair, ethical, and compliant business practices.

Not every financial interest is a problem. The important thing is to make sure it is allowed, disclosed when required, and managed properly. This helps protect fair outcomes for Customers and supports compliance.

Commission

Question: What could go wrong if commission is based only on the number of sales?

Commission is a permissible financial interest. However, it cannot be based only on how many products are sold.

When commission rewards quantity alone, there is a risk that sales may be prioritised over the Customer's needs. This can lead to poor Customer outcomes and increased compliance risk.

To support fair outcomes, commission should consider both:

  • The number of sales made.
  • The quality of the Customer interaction.

Quality measures may include fair Customer outcomes, compliance with the FRG Minimum Service Standards, and adherence to the Code of Conduct. Approved disclosures and quality monitoring through CallBi help ensure these standards are met.

Financial interests are not limited to commission.

While commission is one example of a permissible financial interest, Financial Services Providers may also charge certain fees for services performed. These fees are subject to specific rules and must always support fair Customer outcomes.

Understanding Fees

Financial Services Providers may charge a range of fees depending on the services being performed.

Examples include:

  • Binder fees
  • Customer service fees
  • Product supplier service fees
  • Training and data analytics fees

However, all fees must follow important principles:

  • Must be reasonable
  • Must be proportionate to the service provided
  • Must not duplicate payment for the same service
  • Must not negatively affect fair Customer outcomes
  • Any related conflicts of interest must be managed appropriately

Customers must also agree in writing to any applicable service fees and retain the right to cancel these services.

For example, R 115 for claims support to be paid via debit order on the 1st of every month - or some version of this language incorporated into the t&cs.

NOTE! Customers must be able to cancel payment for these services at their discretion.

Apply it: If a low-cost policy attracts a very high administration fee, what should you question?

Consider whether the fee is reasonable and proportionate to the service being provided.

Immaterial Financial Interest

An immaterial financial interest is a financial interest with a value of less than R1 000. This threshold is measured over a calendar year.

Not every financial interest creates a conflict of interest. In some cases, a financial interest may be considered immaterial, meaning it presents a lower risk of influencing decision-making.

Immaterial Financial Interests

Financial interests below R1 000.

May include gifts received during the year (which all amount to R750 rand without having a conflict of interest).

You may also receive 1 item to the value of R750 without this creating a conflict of interest.

Material Financial Interests

Exceed R1 000 either as a single item or cumulatively during the year.

Present a higher risk of creating a conflict of interest.

Even where an interest is considered immaterial, all gifts must still be disclosed in accordance with TFG's Gift Policy.

Remember what your responsibilities are when a conflict arises:

1

Recognise the Interest

2

Consider the Risk

3

Disclose the Interest

4

Allow Assessment

5

Follow the Guidance Provided

Knowledge Check

You receive a gift worth R750 from an organisation that works with TFG Insure. What should you do?

Correct. Gifts and other interests must be disclosed in accordance with TFG's Gift Policy using the appropriate process. This ensures that any potential conflicts of interest can be assessed and managed appropriately, regardless of the gift's value.

Not quite. Employees should not decide for themselves whether a gift is important enough to disclose, delay disclosure until a later date, or rely on others to determine whether disclosure is necessary. Gifts must be disclosed through the appropriate process in accordance with TFG's Gift Policy so that any potential conflicts of interest can be assessed and managed appropriately.

Conflict of Interest in Practice

Review the examples below to see how real-world situations may create actual, potential, or perceived conflicts of interest, and how TFG manages these risks through disclosure and transparency.

Select each scenario to explore how potential conflicts of interest can arise and how they should be disclosed and managed.

Understanding conflicts of interest is only the first step. In practice, situations can change over time, and an interest that was previously disclosed may require further action.

Influencer Marketing

  • You are involved in social media influencing as a secondary (or even primary) source of income will need to disclose this in terms of the Disclosure of Interest Policy
  • TFG may decide that this ‘side-hustle’ is permissible and you are allowed to continue with this source of income while also employed at TFG
  • 3 months after this disclosure is made, MRP approaches you to market their Family Funeral Plan for a lucrative incentive of R 30 000 for the campaign and a discount code which pays you 10% for each sale concluded using your code
  • Whether or not you have become biased and believe that our Customers should be purchasing this product instead of the TFG Funeral Plan, and whether or not you are directly benefiting per sale that is made, entering into this partnership may create the impression of a conflict or be perceived as a conflict and will therefore need to be disclosed again under the Conflict of Interest Management Policy.
  • After the disclosure is made, TFG can make a decision on how we can best manage the conflict and whether or not this is something which must be disclosed to our customer

TFG has a cell captive arrangement with Guardrisk, who is our product supplier

While this relationship does not create a conflict of interest, TFG acknowledges that it may be perceived as a conflict of interest and therefore we (and thereby you as our agents) disclose this arrangement to all of our Customers.

Ad Hoc Disclosures

  • Ad hoc disclosures are event driven and go beyond your standard disclosure wording
  • The following example will demonstrate TFG’s commitment to ongoing conflict of interest management
  • This example shows us that conflict of interest management is not a once off exercise and has to be considered at all junctures
  • While the content of this disclosure is not important for our session, it is important to note that the situation which arose created a perceived conflict of interest and TFG made the decision to manage this conflict using transparency and making an appropriate disclosure to affected Customers
  • The disclosure was made by sending Customers a letter together with an updated Policy and Disclosure Notice containing the disclosure.

NOTE!

What can we learn from this example?

This example demonstrates that conflict of interest management is an ongoing process.

Even when a conflict arises after a product has been sold or a Customer relationship has begun, TFG may take additional steps to manage the situation through transparency and appropriate disclosure.

The important point is not the specific wording of the letter, but understanding that actual, potential, and perceived conflicts of interest must be identified and managed whenever they arise.

Reflection Question

Why did TFG provide this additional disclosure to Customers?

  1. Because conflict of interest disclosures are only required once a year.
  2. Because new situations may create actual, potential, or perceived conflicts that need to be managed transparently.
  3. Because all Customer communications must contain a Conflict of Interest statement.
  4. Because the original disclosure was incorrect.

You now understand which financial interests may be permissible, when disclosure is required, and why actual, potential, or perceived conflicts must be managed transparently.
